title: New England Clam Chowder
subtitle: creamy potato and seafood soup
excerpt: A thick, creamy chowder built on clams, potato, and bacon. It comes together in one pot and takes about 40 minutes from start to finish. Serve with crusty bread for a filling meal.
sourceNotes: New England clam chowder is the signature dish of coastal Massachusetts and Rhode Island. White and cream-based, it has been a staple since the 18th century.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the chowder base a day ahead and store in the fridge. Add the seafood when reheating gently.

content.text: Cook the bacon first so it renders fat into the pot. Use that fat to sweat the vegetables. This builds a deep base flavour before any liquid goes in.
Put a large saucepan over medium heat. Add the bacon and cook for 5 minutes, stirring often, until the fat renders and the bacon starts to colour.
Add the butter, onion, and celery to the pan. Cook for 6 minutes until soft. Stir regularly.
Sprinkle in the flour and stir for 1 minute until it coats the vegetables.
Pour in the fish stock a little at a time, stirring after each addition to prevent lumps. Add the bay leaves.
Add the potato cubes. Bring to a gentle boil, then reduce heat and simmer for 15 minutes until the potatoes are tender.
Pour in the milk and cream. Stir gently and bring back to a simmer over low heat. Do not boil.
Add the clams or prawns. Cook for 3 to 5 minutes until the seafood is just cooked through. Remove bay leaves.
Season with salt and black pepper. Ladle into bowls and serve hot.

items.cause: Not enough flour or the roux cooked too briefly
items.fix: Mix 1 tbsp soft butter with 1 tbsp flour and stir into the simmering soup in small pieces until it thickens.

items.cause: Overcooked -- clams and prawns only need a few minutes
items.fix: Add seafood at the very end and remove from heat as soon as it is cooked through.
Keep the heat low after adding dairy. A bare simmer is all that is needed.

content.text: New England clam chowder comes from the coastal states of the north-eastern United States. Massachusetts and Rhode Island have long competed over who makes it best. The cream-based version is the one most people know today. It has been a staple in waterfront restaurants and home kitchens since the 1700s.
